Another approach may be that the transport service within a district is freely available to all—in much the same way that elevators, escalators, or moving walkways function in large buildings and facilities—with related costs absorbed in the operational budget of the facility. The business case for AMDs relies on the concentrated demand for mobility services in the district in which the automated mobility services are deployed, with perhaps all or a portion of the costs of AMD services absorbed within the overall operating budget of the development in a manner similar to elevators, escalators and other public conveniences, addressing the failure of 6 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. existing modes to provide high-quality service. AMDs are envisioned as being able to improve mobility for people who reside or work in the area served by improving user access and convenience, reducing costs at multiple scales, and creating a new paradigm for mobility. This is done in part by reducing traffic and parking congestion, emissions, and barriers to accessibility— all of which helps justify district-level AMD implementations where the relatively high capital cost of the AV fleets, operations centers, supplemental infrastructure, and associated staff supporting fully automated modes will be primarily driven by (and amortized over) the high density of trips that begin and end within the same district and their associated economic activities. 2.3 Blended AV Transport for Complete Mobility AV and electric drivetrain technologies (battery electric and hydrogen fuel cell electric), as well as other alternative fuels, are being applied to a variety of vehicle sizes and types. Likewise, the integration of these technologies into public transport spans the spectrum of vehicle sizes and types, service modes, and vehicle dispatching concepts. With respect to vehicle sizes and classes, automation and electrification have applications ranging from small automotive classes of vehicles to larger minivan and van classes in addition to classic medium- to large-size buses. The AV fleet emphasis for AMDs is primarily on small- and medium-sized vehicles to provide for community circulation and FMLM service to regional transit services that typically use medium- to large-sized vehicles. Public transit ridership service has traditionally been associated with fixed-schedule, fixed-route systems served by buses and light rail but is now expanding to include real-time, “demand response” dispatching similar to ride-hailing. With business models and technology initially seeded by the ride-hailing industry, public mobility equivalents are becoming prevalent. This form of on-demand transit (ODT) mobility (referred to as microtransit in some contexts) efficiently serves trips with relatively close origins and destinations within a defined area. Such services are being rapidly adopted in low- to mid-density environments spanning rural, exurban, and suburban environments where fixed-route, fixed-schedule traditional transit is impractical or inefficient. Even urbanized areas with well-established regional transit based on fixed-route, fixed-schedule bus or rail technology are beginning to integrate ODT to service lower-density suburbs where fixed-route service is inefficient and provide community circulation services in high-density regions and connection to larger-vehicle regional transit services.
